body.text: Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has indicated the Coalition will largely preference One Nation ahead of Labor and the Greens on how-to-vote cards in Victoria's state election.
As the parties ramp up campaigning, the Big Build royal commission has begun calling its first witnesses in public hearings in Melbourne.

In focus: Native timber logging
Victoria's native timber industry is a key issue in this election, particularly for residents in regions like Gippsland in the state's east.
Labor enacted a ban on native logging in state forests in 2024, following campaigns from conservationists.
It committed $1.5 billion to a program supporting forestry workers transitioning to other industries, which ended in June this year.

But residents in areas reliant on the timber industry say towns have been devastated by the ban, while a Victorian auditor general's report into the end of the industry critiqued the government's transition plan and found a 25 per cent decline in full-time employment among workers.
Others say the native timber logging ban has failed to protect the environment, with logging still taking place "by stealth".
The issue has split parties down political lines.
Labor and the Greens have committed to maintaining the ban on native timber logging, with Labor saying it was continuing to back forestry workers to find new jobs.
The Coalition and One Nation have both pledges to change things, with the Coalition pledging to process native timber at local sawmills under a new forest management program.
One Nation says it will revive native forest logging, but had no details on how it would do so, saying it would consult with industry leaders first.
For voters in electorate with timber ties like Narracan, native logging will continue to loom large as a key policy issue.
Clare's Law plan leaves out children, advocate says
Labor's announcement that it will introduce Clare's Law has drawn a mixed response from one organisation that advocates for children recovering from trauma.
Australian Childhood Foundation says there is a "glaring absence of children and young people" in the government's plan.
The foundation's Conor Pall expressed concern that there's no dedicated pathway to specialist support for children experiencing violence in their homes.

"Adults will be able to ask police whether their partner has a violent past. Children living with family violence don't need a police check. They already know. What they need is somewhere to turn," he says. "We cannot keep telling children to speak up and then have nowhere for them to go when they do."

In focus: Benambra
We're taking an up-close look at every electorate in the coming state election.
Electorate
Rural seat on the NSW border along the Murray River with majority of its population in Wodonga.
Held by
Liberal (13.3 per cent) — Liberal MP Bill Tilley is retiring, having held the seat since 2006.
Benambra has been held by conservative parties continuously since 1877.
Contest
It was a tight contest between the Liberals and an independent in 2022, but neither of those candidates is standing in 2026.
Analysis

Benambra is a deeply conservative rural seat. After more than 40 years of Country and National Party dominance, the Liberals won the seat in 1976. Except for the Labor "Brackslide" of 2002, at which the two-party preferred margin slipped to 4 per cent, Labor has never come close to winning the seat.

In 2018, the Liberals faced their strongest challenge since first gaining Benambra. The party's primary vote tumbled by almost 15 percentage points, and among a crowded field, independent Jacqui Hawkins emerged in second place. In her second run at the seat, she cut the Liberal margin to under 1 per cent.
Benambra is entirely contained within the federal seat of Indi, and Hawkins had previously worked on the successful campaigns of former MP Cathy McGowan and her successor Helen Haines.

The retirement of Liberal MP Bill Tilley after 20 years of holding the seat would ordinarily create an opportunity for a strong challenger, but Hawkins has opted not to run for a third time. It is not clear whether another independent candidate or a One Nation candidate would be better placed to win the seat from the Liberals.
Music Victoria welcomes Coalition nightlife pledge
Music Victoria has welcomed the Coalition's proposed reforms to support live music venues.

As part of the announced pledges, an elected Coalition would cut red tape for venues, streamline approvals for music festivals and outdoor events, and introduce a "trusted operator" system to grant multi-year licences for consistently compliant venues.
Music Victoria chief executive Fiona Duncan says the proposed reforms are welcome, but more needs to be done to invest in Victoria's live music scene.

"Cutting red tape alone won't secure the future of Victoria's grassroots music industry. Artists and music businesses create jobs, attract audiences and drive economic activity across the state. We need to invest in the people creating the music, not just the places where it's played," Duncan said.

"Victoria generates $3.55 billion a year from music — around a third of Australia's music economy. Yet in 2026, our state government invested just 63 cents per person in contemporary music, less than NSW ($3.10), South Australia ($1.46), WA and South Australia.
"We cannot keep trading on our reputation as Australia's music capital without investing in the people who create the music."
Key Event
Jess Wilson says Coalition will preference One Nation above Labor
Jess Wilson is asked about where the Coalition will preference other parties on its how to vote cards.

"The only way to change the government is a number one next to Liberal and Nationals," Wilson says. "We have made the decision that we will be putting Labor, the Greens, the Socialists at the bottom of the ticket and all other parties above that."
"The only way to change the government is a number one next to Liberal and Nationals," Wilson says.
"We have made the decision that we will be putting Labor, the Greens, the Socialists at the bottom of the ticket and all other parties above that."
But Wilson says it will be on a case-by-case and electorate-by-electorate basis, and says the party will be doing due diligence on each candidate.
National Liberal leader on the campaign trail with Jess Wilson
National Liberal leader Angus Taylor says Jess Wilson represents a "fresh start" for Victoria.
"In 18 days' time, Victorians will get an opportunity to vote for that fresh start, and Victoria needs it," Taylor says.
Taylor says he is particularly excited by the Victorian Liberal announcement of support for live music venues.

"I am a child of the 80s. I saw that extraordinary era of 80s rock, live venues that we had that have disappeared," he says. "And I am so pleased to see this announcement here today, because it is so in line with where we are going as a federal opposition."
"I am a child of the 80s. I saw that extraordinary era of 80s rock, live venues that we had that have disappeared," he says.
"And I am so pleased to see this announcement here today, because it is so in line with where we are going as a federal opposition."
Opposition leader makes trip to pub

Liberal party leader Jess Wilson has made a press stop at a pub on Chapel Street in South Yarra today, joined by national Liberal leader Angus Taylor along with MPs Rachel Westaway, David Southwick and Tim McCurdy.
It's part of a policy announcement from the Coalition aimed at revitalising Victorian nightlife.
The opposition is promising a six-week turnaround for liquor licences and a cut to red tape for businesses.
"Victorian venues are paying for a pint and they're getting a pot when it comes to doing business in Victoria," Southwick says.
He says one in four live music venues in Melbourne have closed since 2019.
Key Event
1,037 candidates to contest state election
More than 1,000 candidates have officially nominated to contest the state election
The Victorian Electoral Commission has described the November 28 poll as the "biggest and most complex state election yet".
Nominations closed at 12 noon on Monday, with 734 candidates confirmed for the lower house (Legislative Assembly) and 303 for the upper house (Legislative Council).
Electoral commissioner Sven Bluemmel says all candidates for the 88 lower house seats and eight upper house electorates are listed on the VEC website.

"Your vote is your opportunity to have your say about who you want to represent you in the 61st Parliament of Victoria. Do your own research, check your voting options and make your vote count," Mr Bluemmel says.
One Nation Vic leader will consult Pauline Hanson
One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering says he will consult with national leader Pauline Hanson on Victorian issues where appropriate.
Pickering faced questions this morning from 774 ABC Melbourne's Raf Epstein at Pakenham, where he is hoping to be elected to Victoria's lower house.
He says Hanson won't dictate party policy in Victoria, but he will consult her if he thinks it's necessary.
"Victoria is allowed a certain amount of autonomy to self manage. Yes, we come under the umbrella of the national party and we absolutely share the value set of the party," he says.

"We are better suited to understanding the needs of Victorians than what our federal leadership is [but] if I think there is anything that might be some sort of conflict that I need clarification on I will absolutely run it past our federal leadership."
In focus: Bellarine
Electorate
Held by
Labor (8.5 per cent) — Labor MP Alison Marchant has held the seat since 2022.
The seat has been held by Labor since 2002, and is considered safely Labor.
Analysis
Bellarine has been Labor-held for most of its history. Between 2002 and 2022, it was held by long-serving Labor minister Lisa Neville, who fought two tough contests during her tenure.

Alison Marchant succeeded Neville as the local member at that year’s election with only a small swing against Labor. The party is dominant across the entire district, although in 2022 the Greens boosted its primary vote in the south-western corner of the seat, recording primary votes of around 20 per cent in polling places around Ocean Grove and Barwon Heads.
Royal commission hears workers forced to join the CFMEU

Away from the campaign trail, the Big Build royal commission is hearing more evidence from Glenn Tyrrell, who worked as a health and safety rep on a level crossing removal at Sunbury in Melbourne's outer north.
Mr Tyrrell earlier told the hearing about the CFMEU serving dozens of safety notices on the Gap Road project in late May/early June 2022.
He says when the union representatives would come onto site, they'd walk in front of cranes and equipment, even sitting on barriers, which forced the work to stop.

He says one Friday afternoon, about 15 casual workers who had been hired through Zoom Recruitment were called into a lunchroom and told they had to cease working for the labour hire firm and transfer to a new company, BK Labour Hire.
He said they were also told they were now required to join the CFMEU.
"That's the first time I joined any union," Tyrrell told the hearing.
He said he had to make a bank transfer $590 to the union for half-yearly fees up-front.
He said he was not given any reason why the casual workers had to transfer to the new labour hire company.
Tyrrell told the hearing that after that, the union appointed its own health and safety officer without any election, which had previously been the process, and that his role was diminished.

Tyrrell finishes giving evidence by telling the hearing that the union stoppages put pressure on John Holland and the workers to get their work done and that more workers were brought in to get the job finished on time.
Labor promises crackdown on smart glasses
Smart glasses, sunglasses with built-in computers that can function as cameras and headphones, are an increasingly controversial topic across Victoria.

A growing number of local councils across the state have already been tightening rules around smart glasses. As the ABC's Ethan White reported last month, more than a dozen local councils are investigating or actively banning smart glasses from community facilities such as swimming pools and childcare centres.
The Victorian government last month announced smart glasses would be banned in all Victorian schools from the start of the 2027 school year.
Now, the Carroll government is promising to expand the bans if re-elected.

Swimming pools, change rooms, community sporting venues, hospitals, aged care settings, and services supporting victim-survivors of family violence would be included in the proposed "next step" of the state's ban on the technology.
Labor says accommodations could be made for people with a disability to wear the glasses, many of whom describe the technology as "life-changing".

"There are obviously those who legitimately use these kind of tech assisted glasses and as part of the consultation and the work … we’ll be working with them on appropriate exemptions," Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny said.
Kilkenny has not ruled out making the use of smart glasses to record a criminal offence.
Leading expert not convinced by Clare's Law policy
This morning, Labor announced it would match the opposition's commitment to introduce Clare's Law if it wins the election.
As mentioned, Clare's Law would enable people to ask police if their partner has a history of violence and abuse.
Leading expert on violence against women, Kate Fitz-Gibbon from Monash University, understands the appeal of the law but is not convinced it will be effective.
Professor Fitzgibbon says, like many pre-election policy announcements, the "devil will be in the detail" and she says there are a few challenges legislators will face.

"We know that so much intimate partner violence and offending never comes to the attention of police and certainly such a small amount of the abuse that takes place leads to a conviction," she says. "One of the concerns that myself and others have had about a scheme like this is that it may lead to a false sense of security."
"We know that so much intimate partner violence and offending never comes to the attention of police and certainly such a small amount of the abuse that takes place leads to a conviction," she says.
"One of the concerns that myself and others have had about a scheme like this is that it may lead to a false sense of security."
Professor Fitz-Gibbon is also concerned the system may be ineffectual if information about convictions is not shared between states.
"The concern I have is that the information may not be accurate. It has to be accompanied by fully-funded, wraparound frontline services," she says.
Key Event
Construction royal commission resuming
The royal commission into the Victorian government's Big Build projects and the conduct of the CFMEU is resuming in Melbourne.
It's the second day of the hearings into alleged corruption.
Yesterday, the hearing was told major contractor John Holland was wary of the "unprecedented access" the CFMEU had to government ministers, as well as alleged threats against subcontractors.
Today's first witness is Glenn Tyrrell. He's a crane operator and has been a health and safety rep on construction sites.
He worked on the South Morang, Mernda and Sunbury level crossing projects as well as working on parts of the Metro Rail Tunnel project.
He says there wasn't much of a union presence at the Gap Road project that we heard about yesterday until after April 2022.
He says that was when between two and four CFMEU organisers would begin turning up and presenting John Holland site management with documented safety concerns.
“They’d just come on site and literally stop the whole job," he says. "They’d have their … paperwork and they’d stand in front of machinery and plant and just tell the operator that he must stop.”
“They’d just come on site and literally stop the whole job," he says.
"They’d have their … paperwork and they’d stand in front of machinery and plant and just tell the operator that he must stop.”
The commission then heard that between May 25 and May 31, the CFMEU issued eight safety notices to John Holland, then another 23 between June 1 and 2.
Labor's dating app crackdown
Labor is also announcing a crackdown on offenders on dating sites and apps, proposing a 10-year-ban off apps for people convicted of violent sexual crimes.

"In a survey that was recently conducted, one-third of respondents were sexually assaulted by someone they met on a dating app in the last five years," Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny says. "Perpetrators have no place on dating apps."
"In a survey that was recently conducted, one-third of respondents were sexually assaulted by someone they met on a dating app in the last five years," Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny says.
"Perpetrators have no place on dating apps."
However, Kilkenny has very few details of how the scheme would work, and says it the onus would be on perpetrators to not use apps rather than actually controlling their use.
Perpetrators would be punished if caught using apps under the proposal.

"So punishing them if they're caught rather than stopping them being on the app?" one reporter asks. "Criminal laws are about punishment, they are also about sending a strong message of deterrance," Kilkenny says.

Key Event
Heckler interrupts Labor press conference
While Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny is answering questions about Clare's Law, a heckler shouts her down.
"It's not a safe seat anymore! Don't think it is. Get back on the bus!" the heckler shouts.
When a reporter asks what she makes of it, Kilkenny declines to comment.
Fraser Rise, where the press conference is being held, is in the electorate of Sydenham and has been held by Labor since its inception.
The seat was retained by MP Natalie Hutchins in 2022 by an 8.8 per cent margin.
Why wasn't Clare's Law passed sooner?
Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny is also at the press conference, and she is being peppered with questions about Clare's Law.
Namely, why the Labor government did not introduce the law in November 2024, when first brought to the parliament by the Coalition.
The Victorian opposition promised in July to introduce a domestic violence disclosure scheme within 100 days if it wins office.
But Kilkenny dismisses the questions, saying Labor went through proper channels to develop its policy.
"What we've seen again and again are promises made by the opposition without consulting with the sector, the sector who are experts," Kilkenny says.
Clare's Law, named after the UK scheme introduced after the murder of British woman Clare Wood, would allow Victorians to ask police if their partner has a history of violence and abuse.
Premier Ben Carroll touring Melbourne's north-west
The premier was back on the big red Labor campaign bus today, making a stop at a park in Fraser Rise to spruik a range of proposed law reforms around women's safety.
Labor has committed to introducing both Clare's Law and Aidan's Law if elected.
Carroll says the government will also turn its attention to smart glasses if elected.

"We're gonna make sure creeps that wear smart glasses, creeps that roam dating sites are banned and kicked off those sites," he says. "There is no place for creeps to be on these sites or to be moving around public places, like where I am here at a sports oval, with hi-tech glasses where they can film, record and watch without people's consent."

"There is no place for creeps to be on these sites or to be moving around public places, like where I am here at a sports oval, with hi-tech glasses where they can film, record and watch without people's consent."
He says the proposed legislation to curtail smart glasses use would be passed before Christmas.

Is One Nation really going to jail Dan Andrews?
One Nation's Victoria leader Warren Pickering faced a few spicy questions from 774 ABC Melbourne's Raf Epstein this morning, as well as a few from listeners.
Pickering denied mining billionaire Gina Rinehart held sway over the party, saying she had no influence in Victoria.

"Look mate, I've never met Gina myself personally. I personally think she's a great patriot of this nation," he said. "In my five years with the party, I've never known her to have any influence with respect to policy development or any of these things."
"Look mate, I've never met Gina myself personally. I personally think she's a great patriot of this nation," he said.
"In my five years with the party, I've never known her to have any influence with respect to policy development or any of these things."
Pickering also clarified that statements from a candidate last month who wanted to see former premiers Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan "in jail by Christmas" were not party policy.
"It's actually a comment that was taken out of context to a certain extent," he said. "It's not an official policy, it's not written anywhere, it's not something that we're going to actively pursue."

"It's not an official policy, it's not written anywhere, it's not something that we're going to actively pursue."
The final question to Pickering involved his admission of past drug use.
The One Nation Victorian leader said people should be given more leeway for their past mistakes.

"Our younger generations seem to be completely disenfranchised and, as a result of seeing no future for themselves, they are being pushed to the extremities of the left and the right," he said. "Now we're telling them through targeted assassination of people that maybe had a bit of a tumultuous 20s that you cannot make mistakes in your 20s."

Victorian One Nation leader speaks to Raf Epstein
Earlier this morning, One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering spoke to 774 ABC Melbourne presenter Raf Epstein at Pakenham, where Pickering is trying to win a lower house seat.
Pickering was keen to stress that his party was "more than vibes" and had a plan to reduce Victoria's debt while lowering taxes.
However, he was not prepared to give any figures on how much his party would be prepared to reduce government income from taxes.

"Cost projections in this state have been vastly inaccurate for a decade now. Very rarely has a cost projection been correct," he said. "Victorians don't need more numbers on a spreadsheet. They need a government with the political will to take decisive action."
"Cost projections in this state have been vastly inaccurate for a decade now. Very rarely has a cost projection been correct," he said.
"Victorians don't need more numbers on a spreadsheet. They need a government with the political will to take decisive action."
He did confirm that his party wanted to abolish payroll tax in the regions to encourage more businesses to relocate from Melbourne.
Pickering also said he would be happy to relinquish party leadership if he failed to get elected in Pakenham and another One Nation candidate was successful.

"I'm a team player. I've been a part of developing this party in Victoria since we were a 3 per cent party, but it's never been about me, it's about developing the value set that we believe," he said. "We're not taking Pakenham for granted, absolutely not. It's a tight-run thing and we've got work to do."

Key Event
Greens pledge $50 affordable tickets for major events
The Greens have pledged to make major concerts and events more affordable in Victoria, promising to launch a new lottery scheme for $50 tickets.

The party has dubbed its policy the Affordable Ticket Scheme, which would mandate that major events receiving state government funding or using state government-funded venues make a portion of tickets available through a lottery.
Only open to Victorian residents, the scheme would make $50 the maximum price of event tickets.

The Greens say its lottery would include events such as the Australian Open, major international concerts and sporting events such as the NFL, with the Greens committing an initial $2 million to establish the scheme.
The party says it has modelled the scheme partially on one introduced by the mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani, during the FIFA World Cup.
Greens leader Ellen Sandell says the scheme will open up events to Victorians who might otherwise not be able to afford them.
"Melbourne prides itself on being the sporting and live music capital of Australia, but more and more Victorians are being priced out of the very events that make our city great," Sandell says.

"These events often receive enormous amounts of taxpayer funding, and many are held in venues built and maintained with public money. If organisers are benefiting from public funding, the public should get something back."
